nameStory: The Common Eider gets its name from the precious "eiderdown" - the incredibly soft, warm feathers the female plucks from her own breast to line her nest. For centuries, people have harvested this luxurious down after the ducklings leave, using it to stuff the finest pillows and quilts that were once treasured by royalty and the wealthy.
description: The Common Eider is a large, robust sea duck that's built for life in cold ocean waters. Males in breeding plumage are striking black and white birds with pale green necks, while females are mottled brown for camouflage. These hefty ducks measure 20-28 inches long and are among the largest ducks you'll see along New England's coast. They're powerful fliers despite their bulk, capable of reaching speeds up to 70 mph.

idTips.label: Distinctive sloped bill
idTips.description: The bill appears to flow smoothly into the forehead, creating a distinctive wedge-shaped profile that looks almost Roman-nosed when seen from the side

idTips.label: Male breeding colors
idTips.description: Breeding males are unmistakable with crisp black and white plumage, a pale green wash on the neck, and sometimes a peachy-pink breast that glows in sunlight

idTips.label: Female mottled brown
idTips.description: Females and young birds are richly barred in warm browns and tans, with intricate crosshatched patterns that feel almost tweedy in texture

idTips.label: Large, stocky build
idTips.description: These are hefty, thick-necked ducks that sit low and heavy in the water, often appearing almost rectangular when floating

idTips.label: Coastal flocking behavior
idTips.description: Often seen in large rafts offshore, especially in winter, sometimes numbering in the hundreds as they dive and surface together

habitat: Common Eiders are strictly coastal birds found along New England's rocky shores, harbors, and offshore waters. Look for them around jetties, breakwaters, and areas with mussel beds where they can dive for shellfish. They prefer areas with some protection from the open ocean but avoid freshwater completely.

seasonality.spring: Males are in their most spectacular breeding plumage, while pairs begin moving to nesting areas along the coast. Some birds may still be in winter flocks early in the season.
seasonality.summer: Breeding birds are present but often inconspicuous, with females tending nests near the shore. Males may form small flocks after mating season ends.
seasonality.fall: Birds begin gathering in larger flocks as they move to wintering areas. Males start molting out of breeding plumage into more subdued colors.
seasonality.winter: This is peak viewing time, with large rafts of eiders visible from shore as they concentrate in protected coastal waters to feed on shellfish.

funFact: A female Common Eider can dive down 60 feet underwater and use her powerful bill to literally rip mussels off rocks, then surface and swallow them whole - shells and all - letting her muscular gizzard crush the shells to get to the meat inside.
confusionNotes: The sloped bill profile is key to separating Common Eiders from other large ducks. Remember: if the bill looks like it's sliding off the forehead, it's probably an eider. Other sea ducks like scoters have more clearly defined bills that don't flow into the head shape.
contextualKnowledge: Eiderdown is still considered the world's finest natural insulation, warmer than goose down and incredibly light. A single eiderdown comforter can cost thousands of dollars and last for generations, making these ducks some of the most economically valuable waterfowl in the world.
compareHints: Common Eiders are much more abundant than their relative the King Eider in New England waters. King Eiders have a more prominent orange knob on their bill and different head coloring in males, plus they're typically found farther offshore. Common Eiders are the eiders you're most likely to see from shore or in harbors.

relatedSpecies.distinction: King Eiders are much more colorful than their Common Eider relatives, especially the males with their bright orange facial ornaments versus the Common Eider's simpler black and white pattern.
